title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media. An AI generated deepfake was used on a WhatsApp video call to present the caller as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay, and the impersonation was the whole mechanism of the fraud. No product failed and no model made a false claim on its own, a person used a generated likeness of a public figure to be believed.

The point of deployment was the victim's own phone, inside a consumer messaging app, where the call arrived with nothing that let the recipient check whether the face on screen belonged to the person it appeared to be. The demands escalated through the same channel, from a promised Rs 11 lakh in aid to Rs 5,000 in exchange charges, Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN, and a claimed CBI officer named Thakur seeking a fine of more than Rs 50,000. Catching it would have required verifying the caller's identity outside the call itself, through an official channel, because the call carried no such check.

What is not established is who made the deepfake or who ran the fraud. The report describes a police complaint and a case registered under the Information Technology Act, not an arrest or a finding, and the single outlet account is not proof of intent by anyone identified.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on September 9. The caller used an AI generated deepfake to appear as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and offered financial aid. The fraudster said Giri would get Rs 11 lakh, then had a supposed manager ask for Rs 5,000 as exchange charges and Rs 18,000 to unlock his PIN.

A person claiming to be a CBI officer named Thakur demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid Rs 18,000 and later sent money through a digital payment app, losing over Rs 1.04 lakh in total. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act, and police warned people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them. This was the first such case reported in the city.
